title: TC0-01561
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (XXXX or Appellant) is a citizen of the Republic of Korea (South Korea), and he is appealing a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that denied his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (XXXX or Appellant) is a citizen of the Republic of Korea (South Korea), and he is appealing a Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision that denied his claim for refugee protection.

XXXX alleges that he suffered years of bullying at school in South Korea because he was Chinese-born, and had a mother who defected from North Korea. He alleges that the bullying will continue if he were to return to South Korea.

The RPD decided that the discrimination experienced by XXXX did not threaten his fundamental rights, but rather affected the quality of his existence in South Korea. The RPD found that XXXX experienced discrimination that does not reach the level of persecution, and concluded that XXXX had not adduced evidence that his fundamental human rights were violated in the past or would be violated in the future.
XXXX argues that the RPD erred in deciding that the abuse XXXX faced did not amount to persecution, and erred in concluding that since he is an adult now, he will not face persecution in the future.
It is my decision that the RPD was correct in deciding that XXXX is not entitled to refugee protection. XXXX does not face a forward-looking risk of persecution or harm in South Korea.
I dismiss the appeal. The RPD was correct in finding that the Appellant is neither a Convention1 refugee nor a person in need of protection.

My role is to look at all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.2 It is my decision that the RPD correctly decided that XXXX is not entitled to refugee protection. I find the determinative issue to be that XXXX does not face a forward-looking risk of persecution or harm if he were to return to South Korea.

XXXX alleges that he suffered prolonged and serious bullying over a number of years during his school years in South Korea. For example, XXXX alleges that the school children found out he was North Korean, and he subsequently suffered name calling such as being told he was a North Korean spy and a burden that feeds off the South Korean system; cruel remarks such as being called stupid and backwards and being told he did not belong and that he should return to his country; and physical abuse such as a being punched in the face, having objects thrown at him, being slapped in the face and being elbowed so hard that he received a XXXX XXXX XXXX. XXXX alleges that he did not receive satisfactory intervention by the authorities, and that the abuse caused him to suffer severe mental effects, including XXXX XXXX XXXX. He alleges that he was told he could not transfer schools, and the only other option was to attend a special school designed for North Koreans, which was unacceptable to him because the quality of education was low and XXXX would have to live in a dormitory away from his mother. XXXX's mother was afraid of him being separated from her due to XXXX's fragile mental state.

The RPD found that XXXX's allegations did not amount to persecution. XXXX disagrees with this finding and argues that he is entitled to his fundamental right to an education free from abuse, and that, at the very least, the various acts throughout the years cumulatively amount to persecution.

I acknowledge XXXX's allegations and his arguments with respect to his disagreement with the RPD about whether the past events constitute persecution. However, I find that it is unnecessary for me to decide whether these past events meet the definition of persecution because I find that XXXX will not face such a risk on a forward-looking basis.

With respect to forward-looking risk, and for the following reasons, I find that if and when XXXX is required to return to South Korea, he would not face more than a mere possibility of persecution, or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk of harm under section 97 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.3

XXXX argues that he will be a high school student when he returns to South Korea and that he has the right to an education free from discrimination, abuse and persecution. I disagree that XXXX will be a high school student when he returns to South Korea. If and when XXXX returns to South Korea, he will have completed his high school education in Canada, and it will be unnecessary for him to return to high school in South Korea. He will be an adult, possibly attending university, and I find there is a lack of information that school-aged bullying extends to adults in university.

XXXX testified at the RPD hearing that took place on November 19, 2019, that he was attending high school in XXXX XXXX in Canada.4 I take notice of the fact that the school year in XXXX XXXX from September 1 to June 30.5 If XXXX was in XXXX XXXX at the time of the RPD hearing on November 19, 2019, and the school year runs from September 1 to June 30, that means that as I complete this decision in April 2021, XXXX is in XXXX XXXX, with approximately two months left to complete his final year of high school.

It is my understanding that XXXX would have sufficient time to complete XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, his final year of high school education in Canada, before he would be required to return to South Korea after this decision. I make this statement based on my understanding that when the Refugee Appeal Divison (RAD) decides that an appellant is not entitled to refugee protection, the appellant is not necessarily required to leave Canada immediately. For example, an appellant has the option to make an application to the Federal Court for leave (i.e., permission) to have the Federal Court judicially review the RAD decision. I also understand that there may be a Pre-Removal Risk Assessment process. These processes take time and would provide XXXX more than sufficient time to complete the several weeks remaining XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX final year of high school education.

XXXX was born on XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, which makes him 19 years XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX as I write this decision. He indicated in his testimony at the RPD hearing that his age is calculated as one year older in South Korea.6 Nineteen is the age of majority in South Korea. XXXX will be 20 years old in a few months XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX.

I find that if and when XXXX is required to return to South Korea, he will be a 20-year-old adult (21 years old in South Korea), and that even if he were to enroll in university, he would not face more than a mere possibility of persecution, or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk of harm on a forward-looking basis. This is because the evidence suggests that the school bullying takes place in school-aged children.

The documents cited by XXXX in his Memorandum of Arguments are not relevant to XXXX's circumstances as a 20-year-old adult (21-year-old in South Korean age). The documents cited by XXXX in the section entitled "The Appellant Faces a Forward-looking Risk" in his Memorandum of Arguments (see paragraphs 41 to 53 of his Memorandum of Arguments) consistently refer to school bullying in the context of school-aged children and teens. For example: a. Footnote 44 of the XXXX's Memorandum of Argument cites a study entitled, "Variables Linking School Bullying and Suicidal Ideation in Middle School Students in South Korea" [Emphasis Added]; b. Footnote 45 of XXXXs Memorandum of Argument refers to a study indicating, "Bullying among school-aged children has become a significant public health concern in Korea associated with psychological and academic maladjustment including lower self-esteem, increased loneliness, higher depression, poorer academic outcomes, and in the extreme even suicide ..." [Emphasis added]; c. Footnote 46 of XXXX's Memorandum of Argument refers to a BBC article indicating, "South Korea firm to sell 'bullying insurance'", and refers to high profile cases of bullying in South Korea in recent years, some of them linked to adolescent suicides; d. Footnote 47 of XXXX Memorandum of Arguments cites an article from the Korea Times, entitled, "3 out of 10 students experience bullying in S. Korea", and relys upon a study of students in elementary, middle and high schools. e. Footnote 49 of XXXX's Memorandum of Arguments cites an article about a Korean teen who suffered from bullying who committed suicide.

I dismiss the appeal and confirm the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. (signed) Derek Vermette Derek Vermette April 22, 2021 Date 1 1951 Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees: Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, "Handbook on Procedures and Criteria for Determining Refugee Status", under the 1951 Convention. 2 Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v. Huruglica, 2016 FCA 93; Rozas del Solar v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2018 FC 1145. 3 Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, S.C. 2001, c. 27. 4 RPD Transcript (November 12, 2019), at p. 9, line 45 to p. 10, line 8. 5 XXXX XXXX School Board website: https://www.XXXX XXXX XXXX/About-Us/School-Year-Calendar. 6 RPD Transcript (November 12, 2019), at p. 17, line 9 to 21, where he indicates that his Korean age (i.e., as at the RPD hearing) was 19 years old, but his Canadian age was 18 years old. --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ RAD File / Dossier de la SAR : TC0-01561 RAD.25.02 (January, 2020) Disponible en français 2 Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada Refugee Appeal Division Commission de l'immigration et du statut de réfugié du Canada Section d'appel des réfugiés RAD.25.02 (January, 2020) Disponible en français
